title: Sorting Algorithms: Bubble, Insertion, Quick Sort
summary: Analyzes Bubble Sort (and the 'swapped' flag that makes its best case O(n)) and Insertion Sort, which is fast on almost-sorted (k-sorted) lists. Both are O(n²) on average. The curriculum's sorting page covers Bubble and Insertion; Quick Sort's example and Big-O (O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst) are on the Big-O page. Step-by-step guide arrives when the lecture is published.
goal: Explain how Bubble, Insertion and Quick Sort work and state each one's best, average and worst case.

steps.title: Read and run Bubble and Insertion Sort
steps.detail: Read the sorting page, then run the lesson's improved Bubble Sort and Insertion Sort on [4, 3, 2, 1] (worst case) and [1, 2, 3, 4] (best case). Add a print inside the outer loop to watch each pass.
steps.doneWhen: You can see the sorted list exit Bubble Sort after one pass.

steps.title: Run the curriculum's Quick Sort
steps.detail: This version from the Big-O page picks a middle pivot and splits into smaller, equal and larger lists.

steps.title: Get pytest ready
steps.detail: The listed assignment (Selection Sort) asks for pytest tests, including empty lists, one item, zero and negatives. Check pytest works before class.
steps.doneWhen: The command prints a pytest version.

steps.title: Compare all three out loud
steps.detail: Interview practice: for each sort, say how it works in one sentence and its best/average/worst Big-O before writing any code. Add the space cost: Bubble and Insertion sort in place (O(1)); this Quick Sort builds new lists (O(n)).
steps.doneWhen: You can fill a 3×3 best/average/worst table from memory.

concepts.meaning: Swap neighbors that are out of order, pass after pass, until nothing swaps.
Take each item and slide it left until it's in the right spot.
Pick a pivot, split items into smaller and larger, then sort each side.
How fast the algorithm is on the easiest, typical and hardest inputs.
A list where every item is at most k places from where it belongs.
